review_basis: Visually inspected each original Module 09 numbered WebP for this part, tracing its actual diagrams, numerical examples, decisions, and caveats. Scripts follow original visual reading order.

scenes.title: SageMaker Ground Truth
scenes.narration: This diagram starts with unlabeled images or text and moves through detailed labeling instructions, human workers, label review, and a finished training dataset. The example below shows an image of a dog. A job asks workers to choose dog or cat, a worker selects dog, and review confirms that label before the image enters a supervised-learning dataset. The choice of instructions matters: ambiguous or inconsistent labels can harm the trained model even when the workflow is automated. The middle panel lists private, vendor, or public workers as possible workforce categories. Read the blue lifecycle notice above the workflow carefully: the slide says SageMaker Ground Truth is closed to new customers, while existing customers can continue. Treat it as an explanation of the labeling concept and check current access before planning a new deployment. The key idea box also distinguishes human labeling from reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF. Labeling examples for supervised training does not automatically constitute an RLHF process.

scenes.title: SageMaker – ML Governance Model Card
scenes.narration: Read the six cards across the top as the contents and approval path of a SageMaker Model Card. First document the exact model version, framework, and configuration. Second specify intended business use, target users, and operating conditions. Third record data sources, preparation, training, and evaluation metrics. Fourth describe known limitations, risks, possible harms, and mitigations. Fifth consolidate that information into a model card stored with model governance records. Sixth let appropriate stakeholders review it for compliance, safety, and responsible deployment. The loan-risk example below names LoanRiskModel version one, trained with XGBoost to predict default for consumer loan applications. Its card summarizes historical loan data, evaluation such as AUC, and limitations including bias risk and unsuitable use outside the intended loan population. Risk, legal, and compliance teams review those claims before deployment. The exam cue is documentation for transparency and governance, not a mechanism that automatically corrects an inaccurate or biased model. A model card should evolve as the model and its evidence change.
